title: Aunque + subjuntivo: concesiones sobre el comercio

sections.content: Aunque takes the subjunctive when you're conceding a hypothetical or a point you're granting for argument's sake rather than reporting a fact -- it lets a sentence admit a benefit (jobs were created, ports expanded) while still steering the reader toward the real point. These sentences are taken directly from the previous reading.

items.spanish: Aunque resulte tentador imaginar los ferrocarriles como simples símbolos de progreso nacional, la mayoría fueron construidos por empresas extranjeras.
items.english: Although it may be tempting to imagine the railways as simple symbols of national progress, most were built by foreign companies.

items.spanish: Aunque estas empresas generaran empleo local, buena parte de sus ganancias salía directamente del país.
items.english: Although these companies generated local employment, much of their profits left the country directly.

items.spanish: Su influencia se extendía incluso sobre la política chilena, aunque nunca ocupara ningún cargo oficial en el gobierno.
items.english: His influence extended even over Chilean politics, even though he never held any official post in the government.

items.spanish: Los puertos se expandieron enormemente, aunque su función principal siguiera siendo la salida de materias primas.
items.english: The ports expanded enormously, even though their main function continued to be the outflow of raw materials.

sections.content: Compare aunque + indicative (aunque es cierto que..., stating a fact as true) with aunque + subjunctive (aunque sea cierto que..., granting a point without committing to it) -- the reading above uses the subjunctive throughout because each concession is being weighed against the writer's real argument, not simply reported.
